events.text: Welcome to the Keegix Podcast, a weekly show about running a B and B, a cottage or a short term rental.
I'm June.
Every fact we use is sourced in the description.
This is episode two, and it's the one a lot of hosts are searching for right about now.
How to get bookings in the slow season.

We'll look at why demand drops, how to set your prices without panicking, how minimum stays and advance notice quietly block bookings, which discounts actually show up to guests, and how to refresh your listing photos for winter.
My guest today is Maya.

Airbnb describes it as adjusting your nightly price based on demand, using hundreds of factors about your listing and your area.

card.text: Adjusts nightly price with demand. You set a minimum and maximum; you can override single nights.

events.text: You turn it on in your pricing settings, and you enter a minimum and a maximum price.

So if you know there's a big hockey tournament or a wedding at the hall down the road, you can price that weekend yourself.

Now, the settings people forget they even set.
Minimum stay and advance notice.
Maya, why do these matter so much in the slow season?
Because they quietly hide you.
In summer, a two or three night minimum makes sense.
You're full anyway, and fewer turnovers save your back.
In November, the same rule means the guest who wants one Tuesday night never even sees you.
Airbnb actually suggests this in its own low season advice.
It does.
Their low season guide suggests allowing shorter stays, and you can set the minimum by day of the week.
So, for example, one night stays midweek, but not on a Friday or a Saturday.
That way you protect your weekends and still catch the weeknight traveller.

events.text: But same day bookings sound stressful.
They can be, which is why it depends on how you check people in.
One host in Airbnb's guide makes last minute bookings work with self check in and scheduled messages.
If you have to drive forty minutes to hand over a key, same day might not be for you.
If guests can let themselves in and find everything on their phone, it's a lot easier.
There's another thing minimum stays do that people don't notice.
Gap nights.
Yes, the lonely night in the middle.

events.text: Let's put this together into something hosts can actually do.
Maya, if someone is listening on a quiet Tuesday in November, what's the plan?
I'd do it in four weeks, one small job a week.
Week one, numbers.
Work out your floor price per night.
Look at your province or city's monthly tourism numbers and your own calendar from last year, and circle your slowest months.
Week two?
Week two, settings.
Put your floor in as your minimum if you use automatic pricing.
Lower your minimum nights for weeknights.
Shorten your advance notice if your check in allows it.
Check that your trip length limits follow local rules.
Week three?
Week three, discounts.
Add a weekly discount and maybe a modest last minute one, both above your floor.
Then leave them alone for a while so you can tell what's working.
And week four?
Week four, the listing.
New winter cover photo, the winter questions answered in photos, and the winter details moved to the top of your description.
Then update your welcome book or house manual with the winter information, so the guests who do book have a good stay and leave a good review.
And then wait?
Then watch.
Check your views and bookings every week or two.
If nothing has moved after a month, change one thing.
Usually it's the price or the cover photo.
One thing I keep thinking about.
None of this costs money.
Right.
Most of it is a couple of evenings with a cup of tea.
The slow season is the one time of year you actually have those evenings.
